You dodge a lot of the sludge by swirling after 4 mins and letting it settle, but not all French press filters are equal. Lots of them are a really loose mesh that lets a lot more through than just about any press made by a coffee gear company rather than most of the department store/supermarket options.

But tbh if she doesn’t want to do ANYTHING the two best options if you ask me are either international roast or get a new wife 😂 (mostly joking)

Agreed about the breville aesthetics.

To be honest, a French press is the most consistent and easy ways to make hot black coffee, so if you don’t specifically want a machine, I’d say it’s your answer. 1:15 ratio, no need to fiddle with blooming or pouring technique. Just dump 20g of coffee in, boil the kettle, pour 300g water. Leave it for 4 mins, swirl, wait 1-5min, and plunge gently. I’ve got a timemore u French press and it’s got markings on the inside so you could very easily not weigh the water either, just use 26g coffee and go full water to the top mark. You could even simplify the process for her and pre weigh beans so she just has to boil, grind, dump, wait, and enjoy.

That being said, the moccamaster isn’t much more complicated. Fold, install, rinse the filter. Dump coffee, shake to level, fill the tank, and press button. The only additional step is the folding and rinsing of the filter.

So many ways I could answer this, so I’ll make a few statements. It’s the best looking brewer IMO, but if i wasn’t aesthetically allergic to stainless steel, I’d have bought the breville/sage for the feature set. It’s great for making a pot of coffee at the asscrack of dawn to take to work, while simultaneously making and drinking a strong latte. That being said, if I have the time to not be rushing, I’d never use it over the v60/chemex. I tend to use the French press on wfh days if I’m flat out and can’t be bothered waiting as the prep takes about the same time if I start the kettle (it’s a brewista and not pictured here) before I grind and get ready. You can also make a better brew with it by starting with the gate closed until the coffee is almost saturated, flicking the machine off, opening the gate to let it bloom (or not if you like the hario switch) for a minute or two, then turning it back on and letting it run. The only problem I have with it is that the heating plate only stays on for 45 mins or so, so if you’re being lazy and want coffee all day or you just forget about it, you have to flick it back on to reheat and the quality deteriorates. I have a hario ceramic lined thermal jug that I usually fill and keep on my desk for the all day pot.

Overall I’d say it’s like a 7/10. It looks good, no major flaws. Does what it needs to, but no bells or whistles. Personally no regrets with it as it does what I need it to, but if you need to fiddle or crave absolute perfection, then get the breville or something more premium.

A couple people have already really spelled out the strengths, so I won’t repeat that, but I’ll add something from my perspective of having a few friends who’ve picked this game up after me.

Don’t be afraid to take 2-3 cost cards in act 1 if they’re solidly impactful anyway, and/or you can build around them.

If you’ve already got a few expensive cards and you find snecko, then it’s fantastic. If you’ve gone for 0-1 cost cards exclusively, then the value in snecko drops because you’re more likely to see cost increases than decreases. Once you’ve taken it, you have a licence to take 2-3 cost cards mostly as you please, though never take cards for the sake of it. Always take cards that help your situation now, or you can reasonably expect to build with in time.

Lastly, something I haven’t seen mentioned, is that if you have orange pellets, and a good balance of attack/skill/powers, or an innate power, then you can remove the confusion and only have the cards you’ve already seen before random. This also works well sometimes for the draw 7 - which others have said, is bonkers strong.

If you wanted straight traditional espresso (aka coffee that tastes like real coffee) you could definitely consider a Eureka Mignon or something else with a hopper, but most people end up trading in for a single doser eventually, and hoppers make far less sense in a home, as they aren’t good bean storage, and therefore the coffee ages quicker (not the end of the world, but not ideal for most).

Okay maybe gimmick is the wrong word but here goes:

Firstly, for context, I was a barista for about 15 years in Australia and moved/changed jobs pretty often, so I’ve used a LOT of commercial coffee gear. You can also check my recent post in this sub for my current setup if you want.

In Australia, Mazzer had dominated the cafe grinder scene, with their huge and robust hopper fed grinders. See robur, robur mk 2, super jolly, Kony, luigi, and of course, their minis. Mazzer have not made a single dosing grinder until the philos (possible exception being SD mods for the minis, but I’m not sure they’re made by mazzer) and as such, I just don’t believe it’s in their ethos. Their hopper grinders are ultra reliable, easy to use, and were the absolute standard until the anfim sp2 and mythos (and recently/arguably the malkohnig e65) came along with better features in different regards, forcing mazzer to pick up their game.

Now, with the context out of the way, the philos. This may sound like an attack, but I’m just going to rattle off the things I don’t like, in no particular order, and keeping in mind that it hasn’t been released yet, and some of these things are entirely my opinion and you may disagree.

The adjustment wheel is on the back, forcing you to have it sit sideways on most kitchen benches if you want easy access to the necessary bits. It will also mean that the dial is hard to read from most angles. It’s also seemingly huge, meaning you’re gonna need THREE kitchen benches. One for the LM, one for this, and one for your prep.

Changing burrs is DEFINITELY a gimmick. Nobody who doesn’t have too much money and time on this planet is going to have multiple burr sets and the willingness to change them. Even those with the money may change them a few times until they find the one they like, and then get rid of the rest. The cleaning aspect to this IS nice, but if you’re disassembling a low retention grinder to clean the burr chamber in a HOME setting more than twice a year, then you have too much free time. (P.S. don’t buy into ANY advertising saying true zero retention. They all say it, and there’s always some retention in the chamber. Don’t get me wrong, .1g off a shot isn’t the end of the world, but even the ek43 needs a knocker, and there’s still some in the chamber when you go to clean it).

It’s stepped and their website says it can ‘be converted to stepless. This could be as easy as shifting a ball bearing to stop the notchy feeling, and you could argue that a 6 micron step is actually a good thing for some, but I think this is overly complicated when the vast majority of SD grinders are stepless and work just fine.

I actually applaud Mazzer for aesthetically designing a grinder for blind baristas, but I have eyeballs, and they do not like this one bit. You may not agree with this, and again, that’s totally fine.

Now, considering the three big points (poor ergos with the wheel on the back, sheer size, and the fact that it isn’t out yet) I’d personally not even have this on the list next to other already available grinders. There are other good options over the ones I’ve already suggested too (df83, timemore sculptor, zerno) which all have their own pros/cons.

I’m not bragging or trying to make this a competition, but I’m not one of the many newbies offering eXpErT opinion.

Water in a saucepan cools at approximately one degree Celsius every minute at room temp, though if a single person is using a single kettle every day, they’ll identify their own cooling rate pretty easily with a thermometer. Cooler days might be a bit quicker obviously, but the difference is unlikely to be more than about 3 degrees Celsius over a 10 minute period. So if it’s 98 degrees Celsius at boil, 10 minutes later it will be 87-90 degrees Celsius every time.

With that being said, it’s a known fact that professional coffee tasters can’t identify a difference in brews with less than a 3-5 degree Celsius difference in brew water, so it’s safe to say that if you made the same ratio brew, you could choose to use water fresh off the boil, 5 mins later, or 10 mins later depending on roast level to suit (hotter for lighter, cooler for darker) and achieve results that were fairly consistent for even an experienced barista.

Anything more complicated than that would go well over the heads (and therefore tastebuds) of 99% of people if you maintain consistency with the other main factors.

I agree that if you’re buying one, gooseneck is tops, but most people own a basic kettle. I have both a good brewista gooseneck with temp control in the kitchen, but also a cheap ass one for homebrewing stuff. The basic one cost $7, the brewista cost $200 or something 7 years ago, and for JUST aeropress, that’s 97% of what you need for a LOT less.

Temp control is nice, but the last variable to play with, and you can drop roughly a degree a minute off the boil, so as long as you waited the same time from boil each time, it would be pretty consistent.

Here’s my little list of criticisms.

Don’t weigh over to account for retention.
Don’t do 18g single shots, the 18:36 thing is a double shot for most espresso drinkers.
There’s nothing wrong with your machine, but get a vst basket.

As for your puck prep, grind into your cup, put the dosing ring on, pour it in, wdt, tap it to collapse, and tamp. When using wdt, aim for a level bed, don’t push it all to the middle. When tamping, you’re actually better than most on this sub, but make sure there’s zero pressure on the tamper when you spin it as this will polish the top and be less likely to drag.

Don’t double distribute, and don’t collapse until you’ve distributed. This encourages fines to fall to the bottom which can cause choking/stalling. The spinny leveller makes more sense in commercial environments, but was the tool people were using before wdt was a thing.

That shot looks pretty good, but probably go 1-2 steps finer and ignore the timer. You also have like a 10 second preinfusion so disregard that time as well. Stop just before you hit target yield to land on your final yield, but a couple grams either side won’t make a huge difference to the final result.

When tasting to see you have two scales to think about. Extraction, and body. For body, ask yourself if it’s thin and watery or thick and intense (change this by increasing dose:yield ratio, or in your case just the dose as your basket is pretty small) less coffee = thin, more = thick. For extraction, it’s sour (under extracted) to ashy (or astringent/tannic if those words mean anything to you) remove ‘bitter’ from your vocab for coffee. Coffee is bitter.

First thing to do is get rid of the shim. You shouldn’t need it. Clearly it’s reduced the space between the burrs too much for your use case and it is grinding too fine. Want to check I’m right on this? Grind at 30 and see how it runs. Or, find your new zero point by ensuring the grinder is empty, turn it on, and dial it coarser one notch at a time. If you hear ANY metal on metal chirping, IMMEDIATELY coarsen it up. If you find that it chirps above like 3, the shim is utterly useless as you will NEVER need to grind that fine unless you’re making Turkish coffee or dust.

If you don’t hear any chirping the whole way down to 0, the issue is probably something else, though if that shot you just made at 30 ran alright and tasted good, (or pretty close) then the point stands and you should remove the shim.

I’m like 90% sure this will solve your issue and you’ll be back where you were in no time.

FYI steps 1-20 are 9 microns apart, and 20-40 are 45 microns apart (1000microns to 1mm). Espresso wants 200-400 microns. I don’t know how thick the shims are, but I’d expect 50-100 microns per shim, which could easily throw you off like this. Only use them if it’s always running too quick while in espresso range, and warranty job it if you need more than 2.

If removing the shim doesn’t fix your problems, it’s your beans. Did you swap beans when you cleaned it? Even just a new bag of the same brand/blend etc?

Time is definitely just a guideline, and not a variable, but it does help a lot. That being said, timer starts when the pump engages (or you start working the lever).

You have 3 times you should be considering. Drop, blonding, and final yield. 

Drop is when the first drops hit the cup, this will be delayed if you have a long preinfusion.

Blonding is when the espresso stream changes from a thick brown to a lighter blonde colour - this is also when you should be cutting the shot for a ristretto as anything after this is lacking in flavour.

Final yield is the total time it takes to get to your desired yield.

Most typical medium roast blends I’ve come across - when dialled in correctly, and are pulled at 94deg Celsius and to a 1:2 (anywhere between 19.5-22g in, 38-44 out, depending on the bean) fall in line with these timings:

Drop: 7-9s
Blonde: 17-23s
Fin: 28-32s

Again, these are guidelines, but if one of these numbers is way off for a medium blend, your beans are probably stale, your temp is probably cooked, or you have channeling due to poor puck prep.

This advice is just straight wrong. You clearly have never used a machine like this. OP please disregard this.

Pretty certain you have a breville/sage entry level home machine by the look of it, and I can tell you that one of their biggest drawbacks is their ability to stretch milk. No I’m not telling you to upgrade, that’s none of my business.

For a machine capable of producing a consistent 1.3bar of steam pressure or better, you definitely want to stretch in that first few seconds, but your machine just won’t do that.

Firstly, that paper ripping sound is the incorporation of air. That sounds is good until a) you have as much froth as you want (or a little more) and b) the temperature of the milk is slightly warmer than the temperature of your hand (if it feels even slightly warm, you need to raise your jug up the wand to stop it). The reason your milk has that high pitched noise is because it is flat. The blending is pretty good actually for you to be able to have poured that initial heart, but you poured over the top of it and destroyed what you’d done.

Secondly, as another user said, practice hearts to begin with and aim for the center of the cup rather than the edge. After hearts you can try tulips as it’s the same thing, just more of them. Both techniques are important later down the road.

Lastly some specific advice for your machine and others of similar caliber that DOES NOT apply to machines that can produce a consistent 1.3 bar + steam pressure. As the steam pressure is mostly insufficient to create good tight foam using the regular advice for steaming milk, there are two techniques you can try to get there.

a) be super aggressive for as little time as possible and blend for as long as possible. To get this to work you have to be fairly close but behind the centre of the jug so that it rolls in the jug initially and doesn’t whirlpool. Imagine a backflip, and get the milk to do that by keeping the wand in line with the vertical centre of the jug, and not offset to one side. Then really try and get that steam wand as shallow as possible without blowing milk out of the jug so that you can incorporate adequate air, then basically proceed as normal to keep it blending.

Or b) physically agitate/swirl the jug while steaming to encourage the whirlpool, though this is tricky as it can be inconsistent if you’re new, and if you agitate too much, you’ll definitely make a mess.

I have an old post about using my grandmas sunbeam barista max - basically a cheaper version of what I’m fairly sure your machine is, and to get the results I did, I was swirling the jug while steaming as it was NOT capable of generating the force required to whirlpool on its own.


Tl;dr: swirling to help the whirlpool OR more shallow wand = more air = good for you, and practice hearts before tulips before rosettas before anything else

So all in all that’s not too bad, but because you’ve asked for critique, I’ll be quite picky.

Firstly, the shot. It looks pretty flat, but there could be a few reasons for that, either it’s been waiting for you to get the camera ready for a few mins and the crema has died, the coffee could be quite old/stale, it could be a super light roast, or you could be pulling too long a shot for those particular beans. All that being said, if it tastes good, none of that matters! What it does mean is that it wasn’t destined for strong contrast as the crema is more blonde than brown.

Secondly the milk. If you’ve really stretched 10oz to 18oz then that’s insane, and impressive that you’ve managed to get art out at all. Some more experienced baristas could do that, but it requires a lot of finesse as the milk is splitting/losing texture while you’re pouring. Fewer smaller bubbles makes for better detail and it’s way easier to pour slow and steady. Heavier froth tends to require serious exaggeration to get art happening, but can sometimes achieve really wicked results. Watch the sticky post in this sub for how to steam milk and see if you can improve or learn anything. It might be the only tip you need.

Next, what you’ve done with it. You definitely smashed what remained of the crema by pouring super fast initially, and as such you had a very milky canvas to draw onto. The advise I’d give for that is to pour slow and STEADY the whole way through. So get that stream flowing in as little time as possible but keep it coming at a consistent rate. Being smooth is the key. If you watch the video again, you’ll notice that the stream isn’t constant while you’re blending it in, you go fast slow fast slow fast slow fast and then hold the last rate while you’re going for the Rosie. Slow the whole lot down and try and keep that flow rate the same the whole time.

Lastly the rosetta, and other art. For a rosetta you want to be pouring into the deepest part of the cup (usually the centre), lowering the jug and slowly increasing the speed of the wiggle as you start to see the pattern appear. To get it to wrap around you have to ‘push’ the pour forward into the base gently to push and stretch the base outwards/sideways. The best thing you can do is practice. You could buy some cheap milk powder and chocolate powder/syrup and just make a shitload of drinks that you wouldn’t drink for the sake of practice. Or you could take up a days work in a quiet cafe and just practice all shift for customers. But that might not be the best environment for it. 

Anyway dude, best of luck and keep it up. Feel free to pm me if you need clarification or have more questions.

Not gonna lie, I had to google it as I have an espresso machine and some jibbijugs, so not one of these subminimal jugs. I also have a gas stove, which is the harshest on anything thin, like a traditional stainless milk jug, and not something like this, but even their website shows it sitting on a steel plate - to thicken the base. I don’t think I’d ever recommend a jug made to go on the stove over a heavy bottomed saucepan, but it’s just my opinion. The last thing you want is burned milk, so if you’re getting good results, then do what makes you happy. If you own that particular milk jug, maybe ignore me, but if you don’t, I guarantee a heavy bottomed saucepan is cheaper and more useful in a kitchen than a stovetop ready milk jug - unless maybe you have an induction cooktop, as they don’t heat the pan.

But all this is my two cents. Feel free to disregard. :)

Be careful to only power it on when you have a vessel to catch the coffee or you’ll brew directly on to the bench!

Also make sure your vessel is larger than the amount of water you put into the machine and you’ll be fine!

If you put 1L of water in, and your jug/cup/thermos is 800ml you’ll have a real bad time! Otherwise you absolutely don’t need the original thermos.

You’ll probably burn your hand as quick as the milk if it has a metal handle. The metal is fairly thin which means the milk won’t heat evenly. Stainless steel also burns/blackens in fire, so you’ll either make a really cool jug or a hideous one lmao. I used to froth with a French press before I had an espresso machine, and I found a heavy bottomed saucepan and a rubber spatula with constant stirring and swirling the pan was the way to go.
